meaning_fix: connections / pull (influence used to get something done); also an intermediary
reasoning: ط is emphatic, so a capital T, and taa marbuta after ط is a. In everyday Palestinian waasTa mostly means connections or pull, not just a neutral go-between.
Urban Palestinian pronounces ذ as d in native words (dahab, gold), so it is respelled with د. Used for golden colour.
Long aa after sh, then warma. The vowel in the second syllable varies a little between speakers, so medium.
Participle of na''aT (to dot), from nu'Ta. ق is a glottal stop, doubled by the shadda, and ط is emphatic T. The initial vowel is reduced, like m-.
Loan from French culotte, used across the Levant, often for briefs or women's underwear (kilsoon is also heard). The final vowel length and the first vowel are uncertain, hence low.
bi- plus yibayyin (it appears), followed by inno (that) with doubled n. Idiomatic Palestinian for 'it seems that'.

meaning_fix: 'five and Thursday': a phrase said to ward off the evil eye; also refers to the hamsa (hand) amulet
reasoning: Taa marbuta after س is e. As said, it is mainly a protective phrase or exclamation, so 'hand of Fatima' covers only the amulet sense.
Palestinian past tense is firi7, with the i-i pattern of state verbs, not MSA fariha. ح is 7.
From Turkish tava. Emphatic T, long aa, and taa marbuta after و is e.
MSA-origin word in normal use. Urban speakers render ذ as z in such borrowings, hence respelled with ز. Taa marbuta after ر is a.
ذ becomes d in the spoken word. The noun is a single-syllable fa3l pattern, though nidr is also conceivable, so low.
ث becomes t (tlaat). The hundreds form is -miyye, with taa marbuta after ي as e.
Turkish -ji suffix on mishkile (problem). It describes someone who stirs up trouble or picks fights.
The dual ending -ayn becomes -een in Palestinian. S is emphatic and ح is 7. Said to someone eating.
Literal 'my eye is red', with 3eeni as the long-ee form of 'my eye'. Note that 'red eye' can also be an idiom for a threatening look or brazenness, but the literal gloss is correct.
shu is the Palestinian 'what'. hal- is the contraction of haad plus il-, and taa marbuta after و is e.
MSA-origin word used in everyday speech, with ق as a glottal stop as in other everyday words. ع is 3.
Taa marbuta after م is e. Common Palestinian word for modesty, propriety and respectful behaviour.
The medial hamza is written '. The word also means head, chief or chairman, as in ra'iis il-baladiyye.
The reply to 'good night' (literally 'and you be of its people'). w joins inta as winta, and the suffix -o is 'his/its'.
Loan word (autostrada) used across the Levant, including Palestine. Pronounced with long oo in each of the first two syllables.
Passive of Salla7 with the it- prefix. S is emphatic, the shadda doubles l, and ح is 7.
MSA-origin but in regular use (munaDDamet it-ta7riir). Urban ظ is pronounced like emphatic ض, so it is respelled and written D. Taa marbuta after م is e.
Palestinian past tense is rikib (i-i), not MSA rakiba. It is used for getting on or into any vehicle.
ishi is the typically Palestinian word for 'thing'. The glottal onset after il- is written per the scheme's rule for glottals inside a token.
